2. In this application the petitioner has challenged the order of the learned Subordinate Judge allowing the application for pre-emption filed under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 which arose in the following circumstances: 

 3. The said Miscellaneous Case was contested by the petitioner by filing written objection denying the material allegations made in the application contending, inter alia, that the application was barred by limitation; that it suffered from defect of parties and was not maintainable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that the lands transferred were non-agricultural lands; that they incurred expenses of Taka 1500 for improvement of the land. 

 4. The said Miscellaneous case has got a chequered career. It was first allowed by the learned Munsif by his order dated 3-6-74 on the finding that case was not bad for defect of parties and that there was no improvement of the land. Against the aforesaid order the petitioner filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 139 of 1974 in the court of District judge. The appeal, however, on transfer was allowed by the learned subordinate Judge who sent the case back on remand for fresh trial by the learned Munsif with a direction to decide the question as to whether application under sub-section (1) of section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was maintainable. It may be noted here that after remand the petitioner filed and additional written objection on 4-7-1975 wherein for the first time he alleged that transferred was non-agricultural land. The case after remand was allowed on contest against the petitioner with costs and exparte against rest with the finding that the case was maintainable under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, that it was not barred by limitation, that there was no defect of parties, that the petitioner could not prove improvement and the opposite party Nos. 1-2 were contiguous land holders and the petitioner was neither a co-sharer tenant nor a boundary man. The petitioner against the aforesaid order for the second time preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 28 of 1976. The appeal, however was allowed and the case again was sent back on remand to the trial court for fresh hearing. Thereafter the case was heard for the third time by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Pirojpur. This time the learned Munsif by his order dated 30-11-76 dismissed the case and rejected the pra for pre-emption holding that the case was not maintainable under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on the finding that land was non-agricultural one. Against the aforesaid order of the learned Munsif dismissing the case the opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 15 of 1977 in the Court of District Judge, Bakerganj which, however on transfer was heard by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Bakerganj. The learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and order dated 28-5-80 allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the learned Munsif holding that the application under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act was maintainable. 

 5. In support of the present Rule Mr Abdul Quayum appearing on behalf of the petitioner assails the judgment of the court of appeal below on several counts. Firstly, he submits that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in holding that the application under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act was maintainable. His next contention is that the lower Appellate Court committed an illegality in allowing pre-emption at the instance of a contiguous holder of land against a co-sharer. His third contention is that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in not awarding improvement cost to the petitioner who improved the land by incurring cost of Taka 1,500. His next contention is that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error in allowing pre-emption in respect of all the plots in dispute although the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 were not owners of land contiguous to disputed plot No.797. He also urges that the lower appellate court was wrong to hold that the application was not barred by limitation under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Now let me consider the contentions one by one. 

 7. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and very strenuously argued that there being existence of dwelling huts, bagan and ditches as it appears from the record of right viz. the C,S. Khatian and the SA Khatian the land transferred is non-agricultural land and application for pre-emption lies in this case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 and not under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He also submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in reversing the finding of the learned Munsif that the land was non-agricultural. From perusal of the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge it appears that while he came to the finding that the land was agricultural land and not non-agricultural land he considered both documentary and oral evidences. He took into consideration CS Khatian, Ext. 5, SA Khatian, Ext. 6, kabala Ext. 1 written objection filed by the petitioner on 31-3-73 wherein the petitioner himself described the disputed land as agricultural land, and the additional written objection filed after the case was remanded by the appellate court. So far as the additional written objection is concerned the learned Subordinate Judge observed that "After the case was sent back on remand the Opposite party No. I filed an Additional Written objection as on 4-7-75 alleging for the first time that part of the case land is not an agricultural land. Evidently this was done in order to frustrate the purpose of pre-emption". After considering the evidences of the witnesses adduced by both the parties he also came to the finding: 

 "I find that the case land is an agricultural land and as such the case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is quite maintainable". 

 8. From the evidence on record it appears that the land admittedly situates outside the Municipal Area, section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act provides for filing application for pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land within a Municipal Area. This section has got no manner of application to case of an agricultural land situated outside the Municipal Area. In the present case the land being admittedly situated outside Municipal area provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has little application. Moreover, under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act a contiguous owner of land has no right of pre-emption. We may profitably refer to the case of Md Abdur Rouf and others vs Ahmuda Khatun and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323, Delivering the judgment of the report his Lordship Fazle Munim (as his Lordship was then) observed; 

 "Moreover, the ingredients of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are different. Some of these distinctions, are that while section 96 confers right of pre-emption on such holder of land contiguous to the land transferred, no such holder of land can exercise the right of pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which merely confers the right of pre-emption on a non-agricultural tenant in respect of non-agricultural land." 

 10. In that case an application under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed for pre-empting some land by a contiguous owner of the land. The said application was resisted by the purchaser on the ground that land was not an agricultural but non-agricultural land and used for residential purpose and as such cannot be pre-empted under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On reading the original deed by which lease was granted mainly for "purpose not connected with agriculture" their Lordships made the above observation and dismissed the appeal rejecting the prayer for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act. The learned advocate for the petitioner was unable to show in the case before us from the record that the original owner used this land for non-agricultural purpose. Rather it appears from the kabala. Exhibit-1 itself that both the vendees of the kabala were agriculturists and there was nothing in the document itself, namely, the kabala Exhibit 1 to show that the petitioner purchased the land for non-agricultural purpose. To attract the provision of section 34 Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act it has to be proved that a non-agricultural tenant himself has also erected a dwelling structure thereon. But in this case evidences also show that there was no structure whatsoever on the disputed land itself. Mere entry in a record of right showing hut, bagan, ditch or pond in plot does not make the land a non-agricultural land unless it can be shown that the initial purpose for which the land was leased out or sold was non-agricultural one. The learned Subordinate Judge also took into consideration the evidences of opposite party Nos. 5, 6, and 7 in order to ascertain the character of the land and considering the evidences in this respect the learned Subordinate Judge as already quoted above found that the land was agricultural land. There is nothing on record to show that this finding is perverse. Therefore, I do not find any reason to hold that this, finding of the learned Subordinate Judge as to the nature of land suffers from any error. 

 11. Learned Advocate for the petitioner next contends that the petitioner being a co-sharer tenant by purchase of plot No. 530 in the holding the application for pre-emption at the instance of the opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2, owners of the land contiguous to the land transferred, cannot be maintained against the petitioner. In support of his contention the learned Advocate relied upon the case of Abdul Haque Miah and others vs Abdul Rashid & others reported in 35 DLR 54(A). But the decision is of no assistance to the learned Advocate as the facts of that case are different from the facts of the instant case before me. In that case the transferee was a co-sharer by inheritance and the pre-emptor was a co-sharer by purchase. But here the petitioner is not a co-sharer by inheritance; he claims to be a co-sharer by purchase. Their Lordships in the aforesaid case on interpretation, of sub-section (10) of section 96 of the Act held that an application under sub-section (1) of section 96 at the instance of a co-sharer by purchase cannot be allowed against a co-sharer by inheritance. The learned Advocate also placed reliance upon the decision in the case of Md Azimuddin Pramanik & others vs Sree Satya Narayan Pramanik & others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 220 in support of his above contention. In the aforesaid case cited before the petitioner for pre-emption was resisted by a co-sharer tenant by purchase. But in the instant case the petitioner is not a co-sharer tenant by purchase as it appears from the finding of the Lower Appellate Court to effect. Whereas admittedly the opposite party No. 1 is neither a co-sharer not a boundary man. "In that view of the matter the principle of law as enunciated in the case reported in 37 DLR (AD) 220 has got no manner of application in this case also. Therefore I held that the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in the facts and circumstances of the case, in holding that the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was maintainable." 

 15. For the reasons stated above, the order of the court of appeal below is modified to the extent as indicated above.
